strengths: The core idea of interactive, region-aware IQA (hypothesize flaws, ground them via cropping, verify by zooming) is a meaningful step beyond single-pass text-only reasoning in existing VLM-based IQA (Q-Insight, VisualQuality-R1, Q-Align), and the motivation from the DiffIQA annotator behavior is well argued.

The GR-IQA dataset pipeline is thoughtfully designed: Visual Reliance Filtering (comparing outputs with vs. without the image) and Hint-Augmented Consistency Filtering address the real and specific problem of hallucinated rationales in VLM-labeled IQA data, with concrete thresholds and examples provided in the supplementary material.

The KL-Coverage regularizer is well-motivated by a concrete diagnostic: existing RL-based IQA models exhibit severe score collapse (2.04% unique score ratio vs. 71.34% for ground-truth MOS). The ablation shows consistent gains (e.g., KonIQ 0.908 to 0.932, CSIQ 0.759 to 0.791), supporting the claim.

Evaluation coverage is broad: seven IQA datasets across in-the-wild, synthetic, and AI-generated categories, reasoning-quality evaluation on two datasets, an ablation over all components, and a downstream application (reasoning-guided restoration with SUPIR/DreamClear) demonstrating practical value.

Multi-turn rollout with GRPO, reward design (format, Gaussian score, Thurstone-inspired rank), and progressive re-sampling for long-tailed scores form a coherent and reproducible training recipe with implementation details disclosed.

Qualitative examples (Figs. 1, 4, 10-13) convincingly illustrate failure modes of competing methods, e.g., factually incorrect 'clear and well-lit' claims, and show Zoom-IQA's verification behavior adjusting ratings after cropping.
weaknesses: The score-regression gains over the closest baselines are small and inconsistent with the 'consistently superior' claim: Zoom-IQA is below Q-Align (0.941) and DeQA (0.953) on KonIQ PLCC, and below Q-Insight on SPAQ (0.902 vs. 0.903); differences across KADID/PIPAL/AGIQA are within noise ranges. The paper should temper this claim and ideally report statistical significance.

Reasoning quality is evaluated exclusively by VLM-as-judge (Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-5-mini). The same Gemini model family generated the GR-IQA rationales that Zoom-IQA was SFT'd to imitate, creating a potential evaluator-familiarity/verifier circularity. No human evaluation is provided, which is standard and expected for this type of qualitative-claim paper.

The benefit of the cropping mechanism itself is not directly quantified. Missing analyses include: crop bounding-box accuracy/grounding quality, how often the crop changes the final rating and whether those changes reduce error, and a comparison against a forced-crop or no-crop policy at inference. The claim that region-aware reasoning causes the score gains remains correlational.

The ablation lacks an important control: Qwen2.5-VL-7B already possesses strong grounding and zoom capabilities; a GRPO baseline on plain SFT data (without GR-IQA-style grounded rationales) would clarify whether gains come from the dataset pipeline versus the RL design. Also, KL-Coverage is not compared against alternative anti-entropy-collapse methods (e.g., entropy bonuses, clip-higher).

GR-IQA (~7,000 trajectories) is built solely from KonIQ images, and both SFT and RL are KonIQ-centric; evidence of generalization of the interactive behavior to SPAQ/synthetic/AIGC domains is indirect (cross-dataset PLCC) rather than demonstrated on the reasoning/grounding side.

VRF discards samples when outputs with and without the image are 'too similar', but a rating can legitimately be text-predictable for easy cases; the paper does not report filtering statistics (fraction discarded, ablation of VRF/HACF themselves), so the contribution of the dataset curation modules is unverified.

Several methodological details are under-specified or only in supplementary material (p=0.02 for the KL mask, sigma=0.35, VRF thresholds), and the work has no explicit limitations or societal-impact discussion; image quality judgments can propagate bias into restoration/RLHF pipelines, which deserved mention.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and well-motivated gap: existing reasoning-based IQA models are single-pass and text-only, while human quality assessment involves inspecting uncertain regions. The hypothesize-crop-verify loop is a natural and sensible mechanism for this task.

The system-level design is thoughtful: the KL-Coverage regularizer is grounded in a concrete, quantified failure mode (score collapse, 2.04% unique-score ratio vs. 71.34% for MOS), and the progressive re-sampling strategy addresses a real long-tail issue in IQA data.

The experimental coverage is broad: seven IQA benchmarks across in-the-wild, synthetic, and AI-generated categories, a VLM-as-judge reasoning evaluation, an ablation study of each RL component, and a downstream restoration application (Figs. 5, 7-9) demonstrating practical value beyond PLCC/SRCC.

The GR-IQA curation pipeline (Visual Reliance Filtering and Hint-Augmented Consistency Filtering) is a reasonable attempt to combat hallucination in machine-generated CoT data, and the supplementary material provides good transparency with full prompts, filtering examples, and threshold values.

The paper is generally well written and clearly structured; the two-stage SFT+GRPO pipeline and reward designs are described in sufficient detail to be broadly reproducible, given access to the base model and dataset.
weaknesses: The central claim — that interactive region-aware zooming is the key ingredient — is never isolated experimentally. Table 3 ablates reward terms and regularizers on top of the zooming pipeline, but there is no comparison against an identical model trained without the crop tool, nor analysis of how often the model chooses to crop, whether the chosen bounding boxes are meaningful, or whether cropping actually improves scores versus merely producing longer reasoning. The observed gains could plausibly come from the structured rationale format, the RL rewards, or the KL regularizer alone.

The score regression results do not support the claim of 'consistently superior performance across almost all the benchmarks.' On KonIQ the model (0.938/0.922) is clearly behind DeQA (0.953/0.941); on SPAQ (0.902/0.900 vs. 0.903/0.903) and AGIQA (0.816/0.765 vs. 0.817/0.760) it is at best tied with Q-Insight; KADID is essentially tied with VisualQuality-R1. The genuine gains are on PIPAL, LiveW, and CSIQ, and the paper should be more careful and precise in characterizing these mixed results, including statistical significance or variance across seeds.

The reasoning-quality evaluation (Table 2) is potentially biased: the GR-IQA training rationales are generated by Gemini-2.5-pro, and one of the two judges is Gemini-2.5-Flash, raising self-family style/verbosity preference concerns. There is no human evaluation of the reasoning chains, which for a paper whose headline contribution is 'reliable reasoning' is a notable omission.

The GR-IQA dataset is entirely synthetic (Gemini-2.5-pro on KonIQ, ~7k trajectories), and its 'veracity' is certified by another model (Qwen-2.5-32b LLMRater with binary pass/fail). This is circular LLM-validation of LLM output, not human verification; the actual fidelity of the groundings and rationales is unverified. The retention rates after VRF/HACF are also not reported.

There is an internal inconsistency: Figure 3 and its caption describe HACF as 'sentence-level, hint-based checks,' but the method section specifies a single binary decision for the entire sample. Such mismatches in a core contribution (the dataset pipeline) undermine confidence.

The downstream restoration evaluation (Figs. 5, 7-9) is purely qualitative with cherry-pickable examples and no quantitative metrics (e.g., NIQE, MUSIQ, or user study), so the claimed superiority in restoration guidance is weakly supported.

Novelty is moderate: iterative crop-and-zoom reasoning trained with GRPO closely parallels recent VQA works (Pixel-Reasoner, DeepEyes, Chain-of-Focus, VLM-R3); the main novelty is transferring this to IQA plus the data pipeline. The paper could better position and differentiate its technical contribution relative to these.

Reproducibility is limited: the dataset depends on the closed-source Gemini-2.5-pro API, evaluation uses GPT-5-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, and the Project Page placeholder is empty with no explicit code or data release statement. Details such as average number of crop turns at inference, computational cost, and filtering statistics are missing.

Minor quality issues: typos ('KL-Converage' in Fig. 2), an unexplained acronym (Zoom-IQA described as 'Zoomable Region Reasoning for Reliable IQA'), and duplicated reference entries ([59]/[60]), which suggest insufficient proofreading.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and novel for the IQA domain: existing reasoning-based IQA models (Q-Insight, VisualQuality-R1) generate text-only reasoning, and Zoom-IQA introduces an iterative hypothesize-and-verify loop with explicit visual grounding (crop/zoom actions), which mirrors how humans assess quality.

The GR-IQA dataset curation pipeline is a thoughtful contribution: Visual Reliance Filtering (comparing outputs with vs. without the image) and Hint-Augmented Consistency Filtering directly target the hallucination problem in VLM-generated rationales, and the supplementary material provides concrete prompts, thresholds, and filtered examples that support reproducibility.

The KL-Coverage regularizer addresses a real and well-documented failure mode (entropy/score collapse in RL fine-tuning) and is supported by a striking motivating statistic (2.04% unique score ratio for VisualQuality-R1 vs. 71.34% for ground truth).

Experimental coverage is broad: score regression on seven IQA benchmarks across in-the-wild, synthetic, and AI-generated categories, a VLM-as-judge reasoning evaluation, a component-wise ablation, and a downstream application (reasoning-guided restoration with SUPIR/DreamClear), which together go beyond a single-metric paper.

The two-stage SFT-then-RL design (learn 'how to zoom' via SFT, learn 'when to zoom' via RL) is clean and the multi-turn GRPO formulation with validity masks over generated tokens is technically coherent.
weaknesses: The quantitative evidence for score prediction superiority is weaker than the claims suggest. In Table 1, Zoom-IQA trails DeQA on KonIQ (0.938 vs. 0.953 PLCC) and SPAQ, and is essentially tied with Q-Insight/VisualQuality-R1 on KADID (0.701 vs. 0.702/0.703). The text's claim of 'consistently superior performance across almost all benchmarks' overstates margins that are within typical variance; no significance testing, seeds, or error bars are reported.

The reasoning-quality evaluation (Table 2) relies entirely on VLM-as-judge scores from closed-source models, with no human study. This is doubly concerning because (a) the data generator (Gemini-2.5-pro) and one evaluator (Gemini-2.5-Flash) share a family, raising self-preference bias risk, and (b) Zoom-IQA's rationales are explicitly structured to reference the low-level hint indicators that are also given to the judges, potentially advantaging it over baselines.

GR-IQA is built solely from KonIQ images with ratings produced by Gemini-2.5-pro and verified only by another LLM (Qwen-2.5-32b), not by humans. The dataset's fidelity, and whether the grounded-rationale behavior transfers beyond KonIQ-like photos, is not independently validated; the claim of a new dataset resource would be stronger with human verification and a clear release plan (the project page placeholder is empty).

No analysis of the zoom behavior itself is provided: the frequency of 'crop' vs. 'final' decisions, how often crops change the rating, or the inference-time compute cost of the iterative loop versus single-pass baselines. Given that 'when to zoom' is a central claimed contribution, characterizing the learned policy is a notable omission.

Several ablation deltas are small and occasionally inconsistent (e.g., KL-Coverage helps KADID in one configuration but Row 2 already outperforms Row 4 there; progressive training gives KonIQ 0.932->0.938), and the paper does not evaluate generalization of the region-reasoning capability on datasets unseen during rationale training with a controlled setup.

The restoration comparison (Figs. 5, 7-9) is purely qualitative with cherry-picked examples, and the main paper switches between SUPIR and DreamClear framing without quantitative metrics (e.g., NIQE/MUSIQ on restored outputs).

There is no limitations or societal-impact discussion, and the contribution type sits between 'Algorithms/General' and 'Datasets/Benchmarks' without being declared; under a Datasets/Benchmarks reading, the missing human verification and release commitment weigh more heavily.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: the paper is the first, to my knowledge, to introduce interactive, region-aware 'crop-and-zoom' reasoning into VLM-based IQA, going beyond single-pass textual reasoning of prior RL-based IQA methods (Q-Insight, VisualQuality-R1, Q-Ponder); the hypothesize–verify loop is a meaningful conceptual advance for reliability/interpretability of IQA outputs.

The GR-IQA curation pipeline is thoughtful: Visual Reliance Filtering (with/without image contrast) and Hint-Augmented Consistency Filtering address VLM hallucination in a way that is specifically adapted to IQA (noting why perturbation-injection consistency checks are unsuitable for degradation-sensitive tasks); the supplementary provides prompts, thresholds, and filtered-out examples, aiding reproducibility.

The KL-Coverage regularizer is well-motivated by recent entropy-collapse findings and concretely targets the documented 'score collapse' of VisualQuality-R1 (2.04% vs 71.34% unique-score ratio); ablations show consistent gains (e.g., KonIQ 0.908→0.932 PLCC).

Evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: score regression on seven datasets, reasoning quality under two independent LLM judges plus a third evaluator (Grok) and a human study, saliency-grounding benchmark for the zoom policy, downstream restoration guidance (SUPIR/DreamClear) with quantitative metrics, thorough ablations (rewards, KL loss, progressive training, center-crop vs learned policy, SFT vs RL), and runtime comparison showing only marginal latency overhead.

Honest reporting: the authors do not overclaim SOTA on score regression (acknowledging 'comparable' to DeQA-Score/Q-Align) and instead substantiate claims where the contribution lies (reasoning reliability, grounding, downstream transfer).
weaknesses: Score-regression gains over the closest RL-based baselines are modest and sometimes within noise (e.g., KonIQ 0.938 vs 0.918/0.910; SRCC gains often <0.01); no statistical significance testing or variance over seeds is reported, so the strength of the core quantitative claims is hard to gauge.

Reasoning-quality evaluation risks circularity and style bias: GR-IQA rationales are generated by Gemini-2.5-pro, and reasoning is largely judged by closed-source VLM judges which may favor the rigidly structured four-section output format of Zoom-IQA; the de-biasing evidence (third evaluator + human study with only 15 annotators on 30 images) is quite small and not detailed enough to be fully convincing.

The 'iterative refinement' is limited in practice: the pipeline supports essentially one crop round (crop → final); multi-round zooming, deeper exploration, and failure cases of the zoom policy are not analyzed; the RL reward contains no explicit grounding/localization term, so the claim that RL 'learns what to crop' rests on indirect evidence.

Data construction relies on a single closed-source VLM (Gemini-2.5-pro) applied only to KonIQ images (~7k trajectories), raising questions about domain coverage, label bias, licensing/redistribution, and generalization of the grounding supervision; the paper does not state whether GR-IQA or code will be released ('Project Page' is empty), which limits reproducibility.

Several technical details are under-specified: how µ and v of the Thurstone model are estimated from a single MOS per image in the rank reward; the exact number of tokens regularized under the p=0.02 mask; sensitivity to σ, α's, and the VRF/HACF thresholds; RL-stage training data size and step counts; Table 4's checkmark layout for rows 2–5 is ambiguous and makes the ablation comparisions (e.g., 'Row 4 without KL') hard to parse.

Reasoning-quality evaluation is confined to KonIQ and SPAQ (in-distribution for the SFT data on KonIQ), so the reliability claim is not tested on OOD reasoning; the limitations discussion and societal-impact considerations are minimal for a paper whose outputs directly steer image restoration.

No contribution type is declared; the work is best read as Algorithms/General with a Datasets/Benchmarks component. Judged under that lens the evidence is adequate for the method claims, but the dataset contribution (GR-IQA) would benefit from broader annotation analysis (agreement with human MOS, per-dataset statistics) that is not provided.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing RL-based VLM IQA models (Q-Insight, VisualQuality-R1) reason purely in text without any visual grounding, and the proposed 'crop-then-verify' hypothesis-and-verification loop is a natural and sensible way to emulate human IQA behavior.

The GR-IQA dataset curation pipeline is thoughtfully designed. VRF (comparing outputs with vs. without the image) is a clever workaround for the unavailability of token log-probabilities in closed-source VLMs and for the incompatibility of perturbation-based checks with IQA, where injected distortion would alter the target attribute.

The evaluation is broad: score regression on seven IQA datasets, VLM-as-judge reasoning evaluation with two evaluators (plus a third evaluator and a human study in the supplement to address self-preference bias), saliency grounding analysis, runtime measurements, and a downstream image-restoration application (SUPIR/DreamClear) that demonstrates practical value of the reasoning outputs.

Ablation studies (Table 4) are reasonably thorough, individually isolating reward components, the KL-Coverage regularizer, and progressive training, and Table 5 shows the learned zoom policy outperforms a center-crop heuristic and single-stage SFT.
The 'score collapse' observation for VisualQuality-R1 (2.04% unique score ratio vs. 71.34% for ground truth) is a concrete, insightful diagnosis that motivates the KL-Coverage regularizer.
weaknesses: The headline quantitative advantage is weak. On KonIQ, the primary training set, Zoom-IQA (PLCC 0.938) underperforms non-reasoning SOTA such as DeQA-Score (0.953) and Q-Align (0.941). The claimed superiority is only relative to reasoning-capable baselines, and those gains (e.g., 0.938 vs. 0.918) are modest, raising the question of whether the added complexity of the zoom pipeline and RL training delivers a substantive accuracy improvement.

The evaluation of reasoning quality relies primarily on VLM-as-judge scores, which is a soft and partially circular protocol given that the training data itself was generated by a strong VLM (Gemini). The mitigation (Grok evaluator, human ranking with 15 annotators on only 30 images) is too small to be convincing.

The GR-IQA dataset is small (~7k trajectories) and consists entirely of Gemini-2.5-pro pseudo-labels on KonIQ; there is no human verification of the rationales, bounding boxes, or 'easy/hard case' decisions. The claim that region-grounded rationales capture 'which regions a human prioritized' is unverified — the saliency analysis (QAGNet-based) measures generic visual saliency, not quality-criticality from human judgment.

The 'iterative refinement' framing is overstated. Based on the prompt design and all shown examples, the policy supports at most one crop followed by a final answer ('tool': 'crop' then 'final'). This is a two-turn, single-zoom interaction, not a genuinely iterative multi-step exploration; the terminology overpromises relative to what is implemented and evaluated.

Several technical components are under-specified or ad hoc. The rank reward (Eq. 5) requires the model's estimated mean and variance of its rating distribution, but the model appears to emit only a point rating; how µ and v are obtained is never explained. The KL-Coverage regularizer's connection between token-level covariance and entropy collapse is motivated by citation rather than demonstrated empirically (e.g., no entropy/diversity curves are shown), and the top-p=0.02 masking threshold appears arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis.

Fairness of comparison is a concern: baselines differ in backbone, training data, and resolution; VisualQuality-R1 was retrained by the authors but Q-Insight's setup is less clearly aligned. The restoration comparison (Table 3) also shows Zoom-IQA has the *worst* PSNR among methods on DIV2K, which is not discussed.

The qualitative examples in the main paper partially undercut the claims: in Fig. 4 the authors' own score rank percentile (50.4%) is worse than both baselines, and in Fig. 1 the margin over baselines (34.9% vs. 35.1%) is negligible — the figures were clearly selected to illustrate reasoning style rather than measurable advantage.

Reproducibility is limited: the data pipeline depends on closed-source models (Gemini-2.5-pro, Qwen-2.5-32b rater), and the 'Project Page' field is empty; no explicit code/dataset release commitment is stated.

Limitations are not candidly discussed in the main paper: no analysis of failure cases of the zoom policy (e.g., crops to irrelevant regions), no discussion of latency scaling in multi-crop settings, and no consideration of inference cost beyond the reported marginal ~0.06s difference.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely new capability for VLM-based IQA: interactive, region-aware 'zoom-and-verify' reasoning, which moves beyond the purely textual reasoning chains of Q-Insight/VisualQuality-R1. This is a meaningful and well-motivated step for the field.

The GR-IQA dataset curation pipeline (VRF + HACF) is a thoughtful solution to a real problem (hallucination in distilled VLM rationales), and the design rationale—avoiding distortion-injection-based consistency checks because they alter the very attribute IQA measures—is convincing and well argued in the supplementary.

The KL-Coverage regularizer targets a concrete, quantified failure mode (score collapse: 2.04% unique score ratio vs 71.34% for ground truth), and the ablation (Row 4 vs Row 5) shows consistent gains across datasets.

Experimental coverage is broad: score regression on 7 datasets, VLM-as-judge reasoning evaluation with three evaluators, saliency grounding of crops (Table 6 is a nice, targeted validation of the zoom policy), reasoning-guided restoration on two downstream frameworks, and comprehensive component ablations.

The supplementary material strengthens the paper: it addresses the self-preference bias risk in VLM-as-judge evaluation with an independent evaluator (Grok-4.1) and a small human ranking study, includes prompt templates for reproducibility, discusses failure-adjacent concerns (bokeh, night noise), and reports runtime.
weaknesses: Score regression results are not consistently state-of-the-art: DeQA-Score outperforms Zoom-IQA on KonIQ (0.953 vs 0.938 PLCC) and SPAQ, and margins over the closest reasoning baselines are often small. The claim of 'consistently superior performance across almost all the benchmarks' overstates what Table 1 shows relative to the full baseline set, even if fair within the reasoning-capable subset.

The training data is distilled from a single closed-source model (Gemini-2.5-pro) on KonIQ only (~7k trajectories). This creates a potential bottleneck: the model may inherit Gemini's rating biases and its diversity of reasoning styles, and the scope/generalization limits of GR-IQA are not analyzed (e.g., rationales generated on other source datasets). Reproducibility also depends on the dataset and code being released; the project page field in the manuscript is empty.

The central 'iterative refinement' narrative is somewhat overstated relative to the mechanism: the pipeline appears to allow at most one crop-and-verify turn (tool: crop -> final), rather than genuinely open-ended iterative zooming as 'truly interactive visual reasoning' suggests.

The reasoning quality evaluation (Table 2) relies on metrics (Accuracy, Completeness, Confidence) applied to outputs in the authors' own structured format; more verbose, well-structured outputs plausibly score higher under such rubrics regardless of factual reliability. The supplementary mitigation helps, but the human study is small (15 annotators, 30 images).

In the restoration task (Table 3), Zoom-IQA achieves the worst PSNR (21.31 vs 22.44 for Q-Insight) while claiming perceptual gains; the fidelity trade-off is not discussed. Also, the headline example in Fig. 1 shows very small ranking differences (top 34.9% vs 35.1%), making the anecdotal evidence weaker than the surrounding claims.

The KL-Coverage regularizer, while effective, is fairly incremental given prior work on entropy collapse (ref [13]) and KL penalties (ref [49]); novelty is at the level of masking high-covariance numerical answer tokens. A deeper analysis (e.g., direct evidence of restored score distribution diversity after RL, unique-score-ratio before/after) would substantiate the mechanism better.
Societal impact and limitations are not explicitly discussed (e.g., risks of deploying unreliable quality judgments as reward signals).
